title: Three Questions, Three Kinds of Evidence

scenes.visual: Title card: Three Questions, Three Kinds of Evidence.

scenes.tts: Three diseases each kill a particular set of adult neurons. How do we learn what causes them, and what might treat them?
scenes.visual: A side view of a human brain outline, grey. Three labels fade in at the edges: Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, ALS. The question appears as on-screen text.
scenes.narration: Three diseases each kill a particular set of adult neurons. How do we learn what causes them, and what might treat them?

scenes.tts: In Alzheimer disease, early losses include neurons of the en-toe-RYE-nal cortex, and of field C A one in the hippocampus.
scenes.caption: In Alzheimer disease, early losses include neurons of the entorhinal cortex, and of field CA1 in the hippocampus.
scenes.visual: The entorhinal cortex and hippocampal field CA1 glow on the brain outline. Labels: entorhinal cortex, layer II; CA1.
scenes.narration: In Alzheimer disease, early losses include neurons of the entorhinal cortex, and of field CA1 in the hippocampus.

scenes.tts: Both belong to the circuit for new memories.
scenes.visual: A small loop arrow links the two glowing regions. Label: circuit for new declarative memories.
scenes.narration: Both belong to the circuit for new memories.

scenes.tts: In Parkinson disease, the defining loss is of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra, in the midbrain.
scenes.visual: The midbrain substantia nigra glows; an axon bundle runs up to the striatum. Label: substantia nigra pars compacta, dopamine neurons.
scenes.narration: In Parkinson disease, the defining loss is of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra, in the midbrain.

scenes.tts: In A L S, motor neurons die. Upper ones sit in the motor cortex. Lower ones send axons to muscle.
scenes.caption: In ALS, motor neurons die. Upper ones sit in the motor cortex. Lower ones send axons to muscle.
scenes.visual: Motor cortex glows, then a line runs down to a spinal cord cross-section where the ventral horn glows, then out to a muscle. Labels: upper motor neuron, lower motor neuron.
scenes.narration: In ALS, motor neurons die. Upper ones sit in the motor cortex. Lower ones send axons to muscle.

scenes.tts: In each disease, a protein misfolds and clumps. Alzheimer disease has amyloid plaques outside neurons, and tau tangles inside them.
scenes.visual: Beside the Alzheimer regions, a neuron icon appears with a plaque outside (label: amyloid-β plaque) and a tangle inside (label: tau tangle).
scenes.narration: In each disease, a protein misfolds and clumps. Alzheimer disease has amyloid plaques outside neurons, and tau tangles inside them.

scenes.tts: In Parkinson disease, alpha sin-NOO-klee-in is the main protein in the filaments of Lewy bodies. Most A L S has clumps of T D P forty-three.
scenes.caption: In Parkinson disease, α-synuclein is the main protein in the filaments of Lewy bodies. Most ALS has clumps of TDP-43.
scenes.visual: Beside the nigra, a neuron with a round inclusion (label: Lewy body filaments, mainly α-synuclein). Beside the spinal cord, a motor neuron with cytoplasmic specks (label: TDP-43, most ALS).
scenes.narration: In Parkinson disease, α-synuclein is the main protein in the filaments of Lewy bodies. Most ALS has clumps of TDP-43.

scenes.tts: Now three questions, each with its own kind of evidence. First, an autopsy tells you what a clump is made of. It does not tell you whether the clump kills the cell.
scenes.visual: A card stacks at the right of the screen: What builds up? (autopsy). A small question mark hovers over the clump: does it kill?
scenes.narration: Now three questions, each with its own kind of evidence. First, an autopsy tells you what a clump is made of. It does not tell you whether the clump kills the cell.

scenes.tts: Now look at rare families. A gene variant passes from parent to child along with the illness.
scenes.visual: A three-generation pedigree, labelled: example, a dominant family. Affected members are filled squares and circles. A coloured marker for the variant appears on each affected member and on none of the unaffected ones. Small note: not every carrier falls ill by a given age.
scenes.narration: Now look at rare families. A gene variant passes from parent to child along with the illness.

scenes.tts: That travelling together is called cosegregation. It is strong evidence for a cause. But a harmless variant nearby can travel along too. A second family, and tests of what the variant does, make the case.
scenes.visual: Label under the pedigree: cosegregation, evidence for a cause. A second card stacks below the first: What can start it? (families).
scenes.narration: That travelling together is called cosegregation. It is strong evidence for a cause. But a harmless variant nearby can travel along too. A second family, and tests of what the variant does, make the case.

scenes.tts: Here is a puzzle. A family's A L S is caused by a mutation in S O D one. Most people with A L S carry T D P forty-three clumps. Will this family's motor neurons have them?
scenes.caption: Here is a puzzle. A family's ALS is caused by a mutation in SOD1. Most people with ALS carry TDP-43 clumps. Will this family's motor neurons have them?
scenes.visual: A motor neuron icon labelled SOD1 family, with an empty space where clumps would be and a large question mark. On screen: Pause. Will these neurons carry TDP-43 clumps?
scenes.narration: Here is a puzzle. A family's ALS is caused by a mutation in SOD1. Most people with ALS carry TDP-43 clumps. Will this family's motor neurons have them?

scenes.tts: No. In a postmortem series, cases with S O D one mutations lacked T D P forty-three clumps. Their motor neurons died anyway.
scenes.caption: No. In a postmortem series, cases with SOD1 mutations lacked TDP-43 clumps. Their motor neurons died anyway.
scenes.visual: The question mark resolves: no TDP-43 specks in the SOD1 neuron, and the neuron fades. Small note: postmortem series, 2007.
scenes.narration: No. In a postmortem series, cases with SOD1 mutations lacked TDP-43 clumps. Their motor neurons died anyway.

scenes.tts: A disease-causing gene need not encode the protein in the usual deposit. In Alzheimer disease, the three classic dominant genes all affect how amyloid-beta is made or processed.
scenes.visual: Two arrows from the SOD1 gene and from the TDP-43 clump point to separate boxes. Label: a gene need not encode the deposit protein. Below, a second row: APP → Aβ precursor; PSEN1/PSEN2 → presenilins in γ-secretase → Aβ processing.
scenes.narration: A disease-causing gene need not encode the protein in the usual deposit. In Alzheimer disease, the three classic dominant genes all affect how amyloid-beta is made or processed.

scenes.tts: Neither deposits nor disease-causing genes alone show that removing a protein after onset will help. Randomized trials in people give the most direct test, judged on how they think, function or survive.
scenes.visual: A third card stacks below: Does changing it help? (randomized trials in people). A two-arm trial icon: drug and placebo groups.
scenes.narration: Neither deposits nor disease-causing genes alone show that removing a protein after onset will help. Randomized trials in people give the most direct test, judged on how they think, function or survive.

scenes.tts: So ask what each finding can show. Autopsy shows what builds up. Families can show what starts it. Trials test whether changing it helps, and what it costs.
scenes.visual: The three cards glow in turn as each is named. Title above them: what each kind of evidence can show.
scenes.narration: So ask what each finding can show. Autopsy shows what builds up. Families can show what starts it. Trials test whether changing it helps, and what it costs.

scenes.visual: The three cards hold on screen.

scenes.tts: Ask two things of every finding. What does it show? And what can it not show?
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: What does this finding show? What can it not show?
scenes.narration: Ask two things of every finding. What does it show? And what can it not show?
